name: Datt-Ruban T-Models
description: The spherical dust solution that Tolman and Bondi's family leaves out. Every sphere of dust has the same radius $b(t)$, each moment of time is a tube $\mathbb{R} \times S^2$, and the dust is free to differ from shell to shell along it. Cut at a shell and joined to Schwarzschild's vacuum, the tube has the same mass however much dust it holds.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Vladimir Ruban worked for a year as a stoker at the Leningrad Polytechnical Institute before it would take him as a student [krasinski2001ruban]. By 1968 he was a research assistant in the solid state theory division of the Ioffe Institute, with one paper to his name, on detecting radioactive gases [krasinski2001ruban]. That September he sent off four pages on general relativity [ruban1968]. Richard Tolman's solution of 1934 was taken to hold every way a spherical ball of dust can move under its own gravity, and Ruban had found one it leaves out [tolman1934, ruban1968]. The usual derivation assumes, without saying so, that the radius of a shell of dust changes from one shell to the next [ruban1968].¶What if every shell has the same radius? In Tolman's solution the shells nest like the layers of an onion [tolman1934]. Here they stack along a line like slices of a sausage: each moment of time is a tube, $\mathbb{R} \times S^2$, with no centre, open at both ends, and of infinite volume [ruban1968]. The spheres all swell and shrink together: the metric is $ds^2 = -c^2dt^2 + a^2dr^2 + b^2d\Omega^2$ with $b$ a function of the time alone, and Einstein's equations send it along the cycloid of a closed Friedmann universe, $b = r_s\sin^2(\eta/2)$, from nothing up to $r_s$ and back [ruban1968]. The stretch along the tube differs from shell to shell, $a = \epsilon\cot(\eta/2) + 2\mu\left(1 - \tfrac{1}{2}\eta\cot(\eta/2)\right)$, where $\mu(r)$ counts the dust on each shell [ruban1968, krasinski1999datt]. Ruban called these T-models, in the language of Igor Novikov's T-regions, where the radius of the spheres can serve only as a time, as it does inside the horizon of a black hole [ruban1968, novikov1964, krasinski2001ruban].¶How much does such a tube weigh? Cut it off at one shell, join Schwarzschild's vacuum there, and an outside observer measures the mass $r_sc^2/2G$ however far back the tube runs and however much dust it holds [ruban1968, krasinski1999datt]. The binding energy of each shell cancels its rest mass exactly, so a new shell adds nothing to the mass [ruban1969, krasinski2001ruban]. Ruban named the cut tube a T-sphere, an object holding "an unlimited amount of matter" that behaves "in vacuum as an ordinary sphere with finite gravitational mass" [ruban1968]. Its surface is a shell of dust in free fall that stays inside the horizon and touches it once, at the moment of greatest expansion [ruban1968, krasinski2012]. Newton's gravity has nothing like it, and neither has the linearised theory [ruban1968, krasinski1999datt].¶Ruban was the second to find the solution [krasinski2001ruban]. B. Datt had it in a paper of 1938, and Andrzej Krasiński, reprinting that paper in 1999, judged it "at least 30 years ahead of its time" and its author to have "chanced upon a gem" [datt1938, krasinski1999datt]. Ruban cited Datt in the longer paper he sent off that November [ruban1969]. With the same dust on every shell, $\mu$ constant, the tube is the homogeneous universe of Aleksandr Kompaneets and A. S. Chernov (1964) and of Ronald Kantowski and Rainer Sachs (1966) [kompaneets1964, kantowski1966, ruban1969]. With no dust it is the inside of Schwarzschild's horizon [ruban1968, krasinski1999datt].¶With a cosmological constant added, Ruban sorted the ways a tube can end [ruban1969]. It is squeezed to a line or to a point when its spheres close up, and it is flattened onto a single sphere when $a$ reaches zero: neighbouring shells run into one another, and the density there is infinite [ruban1969, krasinski2012]. With $\epsilon = 1$ the shells keep apart from the bang to the crunch only where the dust is thick enough, $\mu > 1/2\pi$ [ruban1969]. Krasiński and Gabriel Giono gave the dust an electric charge, matched Ruban's charged tube to the Reissner-Nordström field, and found the shells colliding within half a swing between the two horizons [krasinski2012]. Peter Szekeres's dust solutions of 1975 hold the T-models with their spherical symmetry removed [szekeres1975, krasinski2001ruban].¶From 1971 Ruban worked at the Leningrad Nuclear Physics Institute, on relativity and on the physics of slow neutrons, and one of his two patents is a neutron filter [krasinski2001ruban]. His thesis of 1979 was on gravitational fields and cosmological models with symmetry groups of three parameters [krasinski2001ruban]. He died of heart disease in February 1984, aged 46 [krasinski2001ruban]. Krasiński reprinted both papers on the T-models in 2001 as "a remarkable example that a careful and creative investigation of a geometry that seems to be remote from the physical reality can produce illuminating results" [krasinski2001ruban].

related.text: The T-models with the same dust on every shell, $\mu$ constant: the homogeneous universe of Kompaneets and Chernov and of Kantowski and Sachs [ruban1969, krasinski2001ruban].

The other spherical dust solution. Tolman and Bondi's family needs the radius of the spheres to change from shell to shell, and the T-models are the dust left over when it stays the same [ruban1968, krasinski1999datt].
With no dust, $\mu = 0$, a T-model is the inside of Schwarzschild's horizon, and a T-sphere has Schwarzschild's vacuum outside its surface [ruban1968, krasinski1999datt].

Zel'dovich and Novikov's way of hiding matter behind a throat. A semiclosed world screens some of its mass and a T-sphere all of it, since each shell's binding energy cancels its rest mass [ruban1968, ruban1969].
Szekeres's second class of dust solutions, with no symmetry, reduces to the T-models when it is made spherical [szekeres1975, krasinski1999datt].

Both are dust joined to Schwarzschild's vacuum on a shell in free fall. Oppenheimer and Snyder's surface starts outside the horizon, and a T-sphere's stays inside it for good [ruban1968, krasinski2012].
Ruban's T-model with a cosmological constant and no mass is built on de Sitter space, and with no dust, $\mu = 0$, it is de Sitter space sliced into tubes of radius $\ell\cosh(ct/\ell)$ [ruban1969].

The other spherical solution that the usual derivation misses once there is a cosmological constant: spheres that keep one radius for all time. Ruban wrote it down in 1969 beside his T-models [ruban1969, krasinski2001ruban].
Ruban's T-models of charged dust join the Reissner-Nordström field on a surface that swings between its two horizons, and their shells collide within half a swing [krasinski2012].

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ the proper time of the dust, $r$ a comoving length along the axis of the tube, and $\theta$ and $\phi$ angles on the spheres. coordinates.name: Ruban's Parametric Time

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the active mass, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, the greatest radius the spheres reach
$1$, $0$ or $-1$, the sign of the vacuum part of $a$, whose size a rescaling of $r$ sets to one

Rest mass of the dust per unit of $r$, as a length, $\mu = (G/c^2)\,d\mathcal{M}/dr$ with $\mathcal{M}(r)$ the rest mass up to the shell $r$; the mass density $\rho$ is $8\pi G\rho/c^2 = 2\mu/(a\,b^2)$

Scale factor along $r$, dimensionless, the solution of the dust equations; its derivative is $\partial_\eta a = -\left(\epsilon - \mu\eta + 2\mu\sin(\eta/2)\cos(\eta/2)\right)/\left(2\sin^2(\eta/2)\right)$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(\eta, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $\eta$ the parameter of the cycloid, a number, and $r$ a comoving length along the axis of the tube. The radius of the spheres is $b = r_s\sin^2(\eta/2)$ and the proper time $t$ of the dust has $c\,dt = b\,d\eta$, so the bang is $\eta = 0$ and the crunch $\eta = 2\pi$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Areal Time

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the active mass, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, the greatest radius the spheres reach
$1$, $0$ or $-1$, the sign of the vacuum part of $a$, whose size a rescaling of $r$ sets to one

Rest mass of the dust per unit of $r$, as a length, $\mu = (G/c^2)\,d\mathcal{M}/dr$ with $\mathcal{M}(r)$ the rest mass up to the shell $r$; the mass density $\rho$ is $8\pi G\rho/c^2 = 2\mu/(a\,T^2)$
Scale factor along $r$, dimensionless, the solution of the dust equations; its derivative is $\partial_T a = \left(2\mu\,T - r_s\,a\right)/\left(2T\left(r_s - T\right)\right)$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(T, r, \theta, \phi)$, where the time $T$ is the radius of the spheres, a length, and $r$ is a comoving length along the axis of the tube. The chart covers the expansion, $T = r_s\sin^2(\eta/2)$ with $0 < \eta < \pi$ the parameter of the cycloid, and the collapse has $-\sqrt{r_s/T - 1}$ for the root in $a$ and $\pi - \arcsin\sqrt{T/r_s}$ for the arcsine. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Ruban's de Sitter T-Model

parameters.description: De Sitter radius, $\ell = \sqrt{3/\Lambda}$, the least radius the spheres reach
$1$, $0$ or $-1$, the sign of the vacuum part of $a$, whose size a rescaling of $r$ sets to one

Rest mass of the dust per unit of $r$, as a length, $\mu = (G/c^2)\,d\mathcal{M}/dr$ with $\mathcal{M}(r)$ the rest mass up to the shell $r$; the mass density $\rho$ is $8\pi G\rho/c^2 = 2\mu/(a\,b^2)$
Scale factor along $r$, dimensionless, the solution of the dust equations with the cosmological constant $\Lambda = 3/\ell^2$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ the proper time of the dust and $r$ a comoving length along the axis of the tube. The cosmological constant is $\Lambda = 3/\ell^2$ and the radius of the spheres is $b = \ell\cosh(ct/\ell)$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Kruskal Exterior of a T-Sphere
domains: V = U \;\text{(the surface of the dust)}

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius of the active mass, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$

Areal radius, a length, the solution of $\left(1 - r/r_s\right)e^{r/r_s} = UV$, with $\mathrm{W}$ the principal branch of Lambert's function, $\mathrm{W}(x)\,e^{\mathrm{W}(x)} = x$; its derivatives are $\partial_U r = -r_s^2\,V e^{-r/r_s}/r$ and $\partial_V r = -r_s^2\,U e^{-r/r_s}/r$

coordinates.convention: We use Kruskal's null coordinates $(U, V, \theta, \phi)$, with $U$ and $V$ numbers, and outside $r_s$ they are $U = -e^{-(ct - r_*)/2r_s}$ and $V = e^{(ct + r_*)/2r_s}$ for Schwarzschild's time $t$ and $r_* = r + r_s\ln(r/r_s - 1)$. The surface of the dust is $V = U$, a radial geodesic through the sphere where the two horizons cross, and the vacuum is the side $V > U$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
